title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbook Standards
author: Alex Chen
content:
Summary

This doc consolidates Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review requirements, operational tooling, and runbook authoring and governance. It is intended to be the canonical reference for service owners and SREs when defining SLOs, responding to incidents, planning capacity, and maintaining operational playbooks.

Goals
- Ensure consistent, measurable SLOs across customer-facing and internal services.
- Define predictable error budget policy and remediation actions.
- Provide concrete capacity planning and forecasting practices to prevent outages.
- Standardize incident reviews (post-incident reviews/RCA) and continuous reliability initiatives.
- Maintain runnable, tested runbooks and minimal toil through operational tooling.

Scope
- Applies to all production services in the Redwood inference stack: API ingress, request routing, model-serving (hosted/dedicated/private), KV/prefix cache, datastore and control plane services.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

SLO principles
- SLOs must reflect user-facing expectations (latency, availability, correctness).
- Each SLO is defined for a single measurable metric over a defined rolling window (typically 30d).
- Prefer objective, quantifiable metrics (e.g., p99 latency, successful-response fraction).
- SLI instrumentation and alerting must be in place before an SLO is declared.

Required SLOs (minimum set for each external-facing service)
- Availability (success-rate): 99.95% monthly for high-traffic APIs; 99.9% for non-critical/internal endpoints.
- Latency (p95 or p99 depending on customer impact): API request p95 < 200ms; model-generation p95 < 800ms (hosted), p95 < 1200ms (dedicated heavy models).
- Error rate: 5xx rate < 0.05% (derived from availability target).
- Integrity: model output correctness SLI where applicable (evaluation/QA-backed) with target defined per-model.

SLO specification template (copy into service SLO doc)
- service_name: short name
- owner: oncall/team
- SLI_name: metric (promql / synthetic test id)
- SLO_target: e.g., 99.95% over 30d
- window: 30d
- measurement_platform: prometheus/metrics-collector/synthetic
- alerting_policy: list of alerts and thresholds
- error_budget_policy: actions tied to burn rate

Error budget and burn policy
- Error budget = 1 - SLO_target over the SLO window.
- Burn rate monitoring: track 1h, 6h, 24h burn rates.
- Thresholds and actions:
  - Green: burn < 20% of budget in window  normal ops.
  - Yellow: 20% <= burn < 50% over 24h  page on sustained degradation (6h sustained), reduce non-essential releases (freeze canary rollouts), SRE/owner to investigate.
  - Red: burn >= 50% over 24h or burn rate > 5x expected  immediate paging; pause all feature rollouts; prioritize mitigations and capacity changes.
  - Exhaustion (budget <= 0): full incident mode, escalate to Director; mandatory post-incident review and mitigation plan within 72 hours.

SLO alerting guidance
- Alert only on actionable thresholds tied to customer impact.
- Provide separate alerts for symptom (high latency) and cause (backend 5xx source).
- Use deduplication and suppression for transient noise: require >5m sustained or >3 spikes in 15m to suppress flapping.

2) Capacity Planning and Headroom

Objectives
- Maintain sufficient headroom to absorb expected traffic growth and failover capacity for common failure modes.

Capacity planning cadence and inputs
- Quarterly capacity review owned by service team + SRE.
- Inputs: historical traffic (90/95/99th), growth forecasts (product/marketing signals), change calendar (releases, marketing events), model changes (larger context lengths or new heavy models), and regional expansion.
- Required artifacts: capacity forecast spreadsheet, stress-test plan, burn-rate scenarios, and expected scaling policy (autoscaling parameters).

Headroom targets and rules of thumb
- Provision baseline headroom of 30% for API ingress and stateless routers.
- For model-serving pools, maintain 1.5x expected peak concurrent utilization for critical customers or reserved instances.
- Reserve emergency burst capacity (warm nodes or pre-warmed containers) covering 20% of baseline for ~30 minutes of peak traffic.

Capacity tests and verification
- Monthly synthetic load tests on a staging environment mirroring production configurations.
- Quarterly chaos tests for common failure modes (AZ failure, 30% of GPUs OOS).
- Automated canary verification for autoscaling changes (safety gates: no target change unless canary passes latency and error SLOs).

Scaling policies and rollback
- Autoscaling decisions must specify CPU/GPU utilization thresholds, request queue limits, and cooldown windows.
- Rollbacks for scaling misconfig: immediate rollback if p95 latency increases > 30% or 5xx rate increases > 5x baseline within cooldown.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Continuous Improvement

Program structure
- Quarterly reliability roadmap maintained in eng-sre/roadmap. Initiatives include: reduced cold-starts, caching effectiveness, kernel/runtime tuning, shard/placement improvements.
- Maintain a reliability backlog and prioritization criteria (customer impact, cost, engineering effort).

Measurement and KPIs
- SLO attainment (monthly), mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to mitigate (MTTM), change-related incident rate, and toil-hours saved.
- Track broken windows: recurring incidents with the same root cause require a remediation ticket within 14 days.

Practices
- Run targeted game days before major releases and high-risk events.
- Continuous evaluation of model-related regressions via scheduled evals tied to SLOs.
- Invest in automation to eliminate runbook steps that are human error driven.

4) Incident Review Standards (Post-Incident Review / RCA)

Required timeline
- Initial incident synopsis: within 4 hours (Slack summary + incident page link).
- Post-incident report (PIR): draft within 72 hours, final within 14 days.

PIR structure (minimum fields)
1. Incident ID and timeline (ISO timestamps)
2. Impact summary (customers affected, SLO burn, revenue impact estimate)
3. Detect -> Mitigate -> Restore chronology (who did what, links to runbooks/actions)
4. Root cause (technical and human/process factors)
5. Contributing factors and mitigations attempted
6. Action items (owner, due date, verification plan)
7. Preventative measures and follow-ups (e.g., automation, additional monitoring, runbook changes)
8. Postmortem review attendees and approvals

Quality requirements
- All PIRs must include at least one measurable remediation (e.g., \"add alert X\", \"increase pool size to Y\") and a verification plan to validate resolution.
- Action items must be small, actionable, and assigned; tickets created in the backlog with due dates.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability

Core tooling (minimum set)
- Metrics: Prometheus -> Cortex long-term store; standard metric names with service prefix (e.g., service_name_request_duration_seconds).
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry traces sampled to 1% by default, higher for specific flows.
- Logging: structured logs shipped to central log platform with retention tiers.
- Synthetic tests: global heartbeat probes for availability and basic generation correctness per-region.
- Dashboards: per-service SLO dashboard (availability, latency, error budget), oncall runbooks links, top 10 error types.

Operational features to implement
- Error budget dashboard (service + org rollups) with burn rate windows and automated notifications to owners.
- Scheduled reports to product and leadership when SLOs drop below targets for >1 month.
- Canary automation: must verify both functional (synthetic checks) and perf SLOs before promoting model or config changes.

Toil reduction and automation
- Convert manual mitigation steps into automated runbook playbooks where safe (e.g., automated failover, autoscale scripts).
- Invest in self-healing: detect known failure signatures and execute pre-approved mitigation playbooks automatically, with immediate paging if automation fails.

6) Runbook Standards and Example

Runbook format (single flat doc per incident type)
- title: short and searchable
- scope: when to use this runbook (symptoms)
- owner: oncall/team and downstream owners
- preconditions: required dashboards, playbooks, and tools
- detection: metrics / alert IDs that trigger runbook
- immediate actions (mitigation steps) - numbered steps, include CLI/SQL/commands with exact parameters
- recovery steps: long-term restore guidance and verification checks
- escalation: exact paging flows, on-call schedule links, pager numbers
- post-incident actions: tickets to file, logs to collect, stakeholders to notify
- test plan: how to periodically validate the runbook (frequency and success criteria)

Runbook governance
- Every runbook must have a last-tested date and test owner. Tests are required quarterly for critical runbooks and biannually for lower-priority ones.
- Runbook changes must be PR-reviewed and included in a changelog on the page.

Example runbook: API 5xx Spike (shortened)
- scope: sudden >0.5% 5xx for API ingress for >5m
- owner: ingress-team-oncall@redwood.com
- detection: alert-api-5xx-spike (promql: increase(http_server_exceptions_total[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.005)

Immediate actions (order matters)
1. Confirm alert and correlate with deploys: `kubectl get events --namespace ingress` and check deployment timestamps.
2. Rollback recent ingress config or traffic-split change (if any): follow deployment rollback runbook (link).
3. Scale ingress replicas by +30% if CPU-backed and p95 latency trending up: `kubectl scale deployment ingress --replicas=$(expr $(kubectl get deploy ingress -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}') + 3)`
4. If 5xx origin is model-serving, isolate by routing a small fraction (10%) to a fallback model or region; update routing via traffic manager CLI.
5. Notify Product and Customer Success if customer-facing errors are observed; include initial mitigation and ETA.

Recovery and verification
- Verify 5xx rate < 0.05% and p95 latency within SLO for 30 consecutive minutes.
- If mitigated, schedule a follow-up debug session within 24 hours to find root cause and create PIR.

Post-incident actions
- Create tickets for permanent fixes, including test coverage and monitoring improvements.
- Update runbook with any new steps discovered during incident.

7) Ownership, Roles, and Training

Responsibilities
- Service owner: maintain SLO definitions, participate in capacity planning, ensure runbooks exist and are tested.
- SRE: advise on SLO targets, maintain observability tooling, assist incident response and post-incident actions.
- Oncall: follow runbooks, escalate when out of runbook scope.

Training and onboarding
- New SRE/oncall onboarding includes: SLO fundamentals, runbook authoring, incident review template, and a guided game day within the first 60 days.
- Maintain an SRE playbook repo with quick reference cards for common actions.

8) Enforcement and Compliance

- SLOs should be reviewed during quarterly reliability reviews; teams missing targets must present remediation plans.
- Engineering management and SRE leadership will review critical action items from PIRs; persistent noncompliance escalates to VP of Eng.

Appendices
A. Standard metric names and PromQL snippets (copyable)
- availability: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[30d]))`
- p95 latency: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))`

B. SLO decision checklist
- Is the SLI reliable and instrumented?
- Does the SLO map to customer experience?
- Is alerting actionable and tied to error budget policy?
- Is there a tested runbook for the symptom?

C. Example SLO table (quick reference)
| Service | SLO (30d) | SLI | Owner | Alert threshold | Error budget policy |
| API Ingress | 99.95% availability | success rate | ingress-team | 99.9% (warning) | Freeze rollouts at yellow |
| Generation-hosted | p95 < 800ms | p95 latency | serving-runtime | p95 > 1s (warning) | Investigate model regressions |
